"That's the exact right question to ask, because one day there will be overcapacity and the party's over. Not there yet. You can measure that by spot rental prices for GPUs. Austin on why inflation isn't hitting everyone equally: higher rates turned government debt into a payout for people who already own assets

"Think about sort of money at a very macro level. Let's zoom out for a moment on where the particular flows are going. At the government level, you can simplify it to 2 things, which is money that the government is spending and money that the government is taking in."

"Because all of the ways government takes money in, which is through various programs and mostly through taxes, is one side of the ledger. The other side of the ledger is all of the ways in which government spends money, right? Social benefits programs, defense, like, interest service on debt."

"It's just a net inflow and a net outflow, and the differential of those is the amount of increase or reduction in the money supply due to the actions of the government. If we spend $8 trillion and take in $5 trillion, that's a plus $3 trillion, right?"

"All that money does have to come out somewhere. If you look at the variable that's been increasing the fastest as rates have gone up, that's payments on government debt, right? Who holds government debt, it is largely the investing class."

"Why is inflation not hitting everywhere equally, what is going on with the debasement trade? Why do assets continue to run? It's the biggest, positive plus, and where the money is coming into the hands of people who already have brokerage accounts or who are institutional investors, because they're the ones who own the T-bills, right?"

"Your average, 25 year old who just got a job and only has been out there for 3 years and doesn't have savings, probably a negative net worth with student debt, right, does not have a giant pile of T-bills. But your 65 year old mother does."

Laura: You said, quote, 'A chain may claim to have hundreds of validators, but that number means very little if most of them are operated by the same entities, hosted in the same data centers, or selected through a closed process.'"

"But THORChain itself has less than hundreds. And as we mentioned earlier, there are just 4 operator addresses that control 39 nodes. So do you think that THORChain passes your own litmus test?"

Chad: "Yeah. I think when it comes to evaluating how decentralized a protocol is, number of validators, not a good way to do it. And I'm not citing THORChain as decentralized because there's 115-ish validators. I'm saying it's decentralized because it has 50, 60, whatever the number is, individual operators across the world, which is better than Bitcoin, right?"

"Bitcoin's got 3, like, mining pools together would be 51% of the computing. Same thing for Ethereum. They've got, like, what, 3 or 4 operators with the major validators of Ethereum, and you would have the same situation. "THORChain is more decentralized than Bitcoin and Ethereum, by the definition that you're granting to me in this moment."

"If you look at, like, halting, meaning the ability to stop the production of blocks, you would need 1/3 plus 1. It's something different if you categorize it as, like, a 2/3 majority to control the blockchain rather than stopping it."

"Even if you take the lesser of the two and you do, like, 1/3 plus 1, you can get 4 operators to, you know, stop the entire protocol. I don't know why they would do that, because you'd be burning your own RUNE to zero, which is not really in their financial interest to do so. But theoretically, on paper, they could do that."

$BTDR outperforming most neos and powered shell cos this morning in a weak tape. Some of that is BTC exposure, but some may be the loan Bitdeer's tenant launched today -->

Background: Bitdeer leased its Tydal site in Norway to Volta for 16 years, ~$4.7B of rent (though Volta can leave for free after year 10; there's also an 8-year renewal option.) Volta is a GPU cloud startup founded this year by ex-Brookfield execs and backed by a16z, Altimeter, Nvidia and Michael Dell's family office. It rents the GPUs at Tydal to Anthropic on a 6-year, $10B deal (per Bloomberg).

Today Volta started raising ~$5B with JPM and GS at talk of roughly 11%.

>Part buys the GPUs
>Part is cash parked with banks, who promise Bitdeer up to ~$1.3B of rent if Volta doesn't pay. That's about half of the first 10 years of rent
>(Volta's GPU loan is 6-years against a 6 year Anthropic contract, so Volta's lenders get repaid out of Anthropic's checks.)

Bitdeer's side:
>All in, we estimate Bitdeer will have put ~$700-900M into Tydal counting the purchase, the money spent building it out for BTC mining before the pivot, and the ~$500M left to finish. 
>Rent averages ~$260M a year after operating costs, so roughly a 30% annual return and a 3-4 year payback 
>Bitdeer should now be able borrow inside Volta's 11% since banks now cover half  and the asset has less terminal value uncertainty than GPUs themselves. 
>My guess is 8.5-10%. Cipher got ~7%, but it had Google behind it
>Rate sensitivity: Every extra 1% costs ~$45M of borrowing room and ~$10M a year of interest on a ~$1B loan
>The bigger swing is how many years lenders will count. If they lend against Volta's full 10-year commitment, Bitdeer can borrow ~$1B, about double what's left to build. If they only count the bank-backed years, it's closer to $600M

Risk left:
>Getting built on time. First half due end of 2026, rest by March 2027
>Years 7-10: Anthropic has to renew or Volta needs a new customer for 6-year old chips; Volta can walk for free after year 10

Easiest ways for BTDR to close the valuation gap with peers:
>Close the Tydal debt and print the terms. Size, rate, length, and how much cash comes back to the parent
>Put out one table per site every quarter with MW leased, term, $/kW, credit support, total invested, spend left and delivery dates. We had to guess at Tydal's all-in cost to write this. Peers get paid a higher multiple partly because you can model them.
>Clean up the cash flow statement and the related party borrowings
>Sign lease #2.

Interesting model here per the 8-K and $AEP release

>WULF agrees to pay estimated financing costs associated with construction of Kentucky Power's ($AEP) planned 760MWs combined cycle generation facility at Big Sandy.
>WULF offers to provide $100M in winter bill credits for Kentucky Power's residential customers over the first 10 years off the contract (estimates this will equate to ~$25 per month during winter heating season per customer, with credits beginning in 2029)
>Agreement includes collateral requirements from WULF (announced upsizing the senior secured revolver this morning, from current $250M)
>Kentucky Power will seek regulatory approvals later this year

"Paying the interest costs on 760MW of new gas generation". Here's how it likely works:

Kentucky Power is a regulated utility. It earns a regulator-approved return on plants once they're running, charged to customers through rates. While a plant is being built, the utility is borrowing and spending but collecting nothing. Normally it books those financing costs as AFUDC (Allowance for Funds Used During Construction), adds them to the plant's price tag, and customers pay them later.

WULF appears to be covering that cost instead. The exact mechanics aren't disclosed yet: interest only or the utility's full return, paid as incurred or as a lump sum. Our guess, could be $100-300M over the build, depending on structure. AEP gets paid sooner, the plant goes into rates cheaper, and existing customers don't fund a plant built for a data center. Looks to be in line thematically with what the White House has demanded.

This is not behind-the-meter because WULF won't own the plant. It will pay tariff rates like any other customer, plus this carry. Expect it to pass through to the tenant in the lease. The Public Service Commission filing later this year will likely reveal more details.

David Friedberg: Rising Rates Could Trigger a Banking Shock Right Before the Midterms

@friedberg:

“We've got a rate problem.

In the last 30 days or so, right, we've seen short-term rates on treasuries climb by 60 basis points.

And so this massive increase in rates is obviously going to impact people's ability to refinance their home, buy a new car, purchase things on credit, and the majority of Americans fall under that umbrella.

And I think there's also kind of an economic challenge ahead with the rate problem, and I would argue, as I always do, that the rate problem is fundamentally rooted in the federal government and the insane spending.

And if you look at the impact that this rate is gonna have on banks, there's 4295 banks that have positive equity that report FDIC, their balance sheets every month.

Based on the actual reported balance sheet of these banks, about 95 banks are going to see an impairment of more than 20% of their equity in the last 30 days or so.

And those reports start to come out on October 30th. So the thing I worry a lot about is on October 30th, we're going to kind of see all these financial reports coming out from all the banks, all the lending institutions, and there's about 95 of them that are going to say, ‘Hey, we've got more than 20% impairment charge on our equity.’

That's going to be a massive shock, and then what are the implications of that?

And that's where we're going to start to wake up to the fact that the rate problem isn't just a purchasing problem for consumers, but it may actually have a bit of a rippling effect here in the economy, starting with the financial institutions.

So they publish their next monthly reports on the September 30th ending period on October 30th, and unfortunately, it coincides right with the election cycle.”

The holy grail of investing is knowing how to balance.

When you can take equally good things where your expectation of return is equal, but because they are uncorrelated and move differently, they balance each other. That is how you can reduce your risk without reducing your returns.

You have to understand that the market is a zero-sum game. The consensus is already reflected in the price, and trying to beat it is a difficult game. In fact, it is more difficult to compete and be successful in the markets than it is to compete in the Olympics. We must be humble about that.

But achieving that balance so you can get a good return without losing a lot of money is everything. Most of my own money is invested in exactly that.
#Investing #AssetAllocation #RiskManagement #Principles

My best explanation of the “software factory” is to literally think about engineering output as a factory.

Before AI, software was mostly craftsmanship. The craftsmen were software engineers, and we spent decades optimizing everything around them: PMs writing specs so engineers worked on the right thing, better tooling, CI/CD, testing, infra, etc. But ultimately the throughput of the factory was still constrained by how much software humans could physically write.

Then the first wave of AI made the craftsmen much faster. Autocomplete, Cursor-style coding, pair programming with AI.

Now agents can increasingly take a feature end to end: understand the spec, inspect the codebase, write the code, test it, fix it, ship it. So for roughly the same human input, the output of the software factory starts going up dramatically.

And I think the end state people are chasing is a mostly autonomous software factory. Engineers write a spec / markdown file, define the tests and constraints, and become much more like verification engineers, while swarms of agents run 24/7 looking at telemetry, customer bugs, regressions, feature requests, then designing, coding, testing and shipping software.

But for that to actually work, the rest of the factory has to be insanely good too: CI/CD, tests, fast deployments, observability, security, rollback, evals, all of it.

It’s basically going from Ferrari building cars with incredible craftsmen doing a huge amount by hand, to the most advanced Tesla-style factory where more and more of the production line is automated.

And the big assumption behind all of this is that your product will eventually be as good as your software factory. If your factory is better, your agents can iterate faster, learn faster, ship more, and ultimately just build a better product.

Yesterday I got a bit roasted on X because I said my agent checks me in for my flights, so let me double down: it also helps me book basically every plane ticket.

I just landed in India and they asked for one of those crazy health/immigration forms with passport info, where you’re staying, flight details, etc. I sent it to my agent, it filled everything out, great job, I went back to reading my book.

A bunch of people replied: “I’m a competent adult, I know how to do this, I don’t need AI.”

Which is totally fair. Do whatever works for you! 

I also know how to wash dishes and I love my dishwasher. I know how to write a letter, put it in an envelope and go to the post office, and yet I prefer email. I know how to do mental arithmetic and I still use a calculator.

The point of technology is very rarely that humans are incapable of doing the thing. It’s that our time and attention are better spent somewhere else.

Instead of spending 20 minutes fighting with a PDF, finding my passport number, hotel address and flight information in five different places, I can read my book. Instead of manually replying to three emails just to send my landlord some insurance information, an agent can handle it and I get another 20 minutes with my 18-month-old daughter, Josephine.

I think people underestimate AI agents for two reasons.

First, capitalism has this amazing tendency to take things that were once reserved for rich people and, through technology and scale, give them to everyone. Rich people have had executive assistants forever. Someone books their flights and restaurants, coordinates meetings, answers routine communications, fills out paperwork, reminds them what they forgot. AI is going to give some version of that to billions of people.

Second, a huge amount of economic progress is simply removing friction. Coase would call a lot of this transaction costs. One form takes 15 minutes, one email takes 3 minutes, one reservation takes 10 minutes. None of these things individually feels revolutionary, but remove thousands of them over a lifetime and it compounds into something enormous.

So yes, I am perfectly capable of checking myself into a flight but now I just don’t see why I should.
